issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: Dorothy had always been a meticulous person, with a keen eye for detail that served her well in her long career as a network engineer. She and her husband of 45 years, John, lived a quiet life in the suburbs, content to spend their free time tinkering with gadgets and watching old movies together. But all of that changed on the day Dorothy witnessed a gruesome accident at the city's central bus station. She had been waiting for her usual bus home from work when a car careened out of control into the crowded terminal, striking several people. The sounds of screams and crunching metal still echoed in her mind years later. What frightened her most was the feeling of utter chaos that followed - people running wildly in all directions, no one seeming to know what to do. In the months that followed, Dorothy began to notice changes in herself. She found herself avoiding crowded places like shopping centers or public events, afraid of being caught in another disaster. Even the thought of riding a bus made her stomach twist with anxiety. Her colleagues at work started to comment on how withdrawn she had become, no longer willing to join them for lunch or meetings in conference rooms. Certain conversation topics also became off-limits for Dorothy. She couldn't bear to hear people talk about accidents or violence - it was as if the memories were waiting just beneath the surface, ready to pounce at any moment. Her friends and family learned not to bring up such subjects around her, but that only made her feel more isolated. As she struggled to cope with these new fears, Dorothy started forcing herself to think only positive thoughts whenever dark memories threatened to intrude. She would repeat affirmations to herself like a mantra - "I am safe," "nothing bad will happen" - but the reassurance was short-lived. Her mind seemed to have developed a hyper-vigilant quality, constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats. Dorothy had come to believe that she was permanently an outsider now, forever changed by what she witnessed that day at the bus station. She saw the world as a perilous place where anything could happen without warning - and it was up to her to stay one step ahead of danger. This unrelenting sense of threat took its toll on her relationships. Her husband John tried to be supportive, but he couldn't understand why she wouldn't join him for simple outings anymore. Their friends noticed the change in them too - they used to be a social couple, always up for an adventure; now they mostly stayed home. At work, Dorothy's performance began to suffer as well. She had trouble focusing on tasks, constantly looking over her shoulder or worrying about what might happen next. Her usual love of problem-solving gave way to a nagging sense of unease that made it hard to concentrate. Despite these struggles, Dorothy didn't seek help until John sat her down and gently told her he couldn't watch her slip further away. He encouraged her to talk to someone - anyone - who might be able to help her find some peace again. With trepidation, Dorothy scheduled an appointment with a therapist, unsure of what to expect but desperate for relief from the constant fear that had taken over her life. As she sat in the waiting room, clutching her purse tightly and scanning the unfamiliar surroundings, Dorothy felt a familiar knot form in her stomach. What if this didn't work? What if nothing could ever make her feel safe again?
